calculus: For a function f, what must be true about each input in its domain?
A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. Different inputs may share an output.
Composition is defined where x is in the domain of g and g(x) is in the domain of f.
The area under f up to a.
The slope of the tangent at x = a.
The derivative is the limit of secant slopes, so it gives the tangent slope when that limit exists.
The two-sided limit must exist and be finite for the ordinary derivative.
For differentiable u and v, which is the derivative of uv?
The product rule differentiates one factor at a time and adds the two resulting terms.
Use the product rule for products and the chain rule for nested functions.
If f′ is positive throughout an interval, what follows?
A positive derivative means the output increases as the input increases. It does not determine the sign of f itself.
Apply on an interval where the stated derivatives exist.
What does the definite integral of velocity over time give?
Integrating signed velocity gives displacement. Total distance instead integrates the absolute value of velocity.
∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F′ = f
For the standard Fundamental Theorem, take f continuous on [a,b].
Which integral gives area between an upper curve u and lower curve l on [a,b]?
Each vertical strip has height upper minus lower. Integrating those strip heights gives the area.
Require u ≥ l; split at intersections if the order changes.
Integration by parts reverses which differentiation rule?
Integrating the product rule d(uv) = u dv + v du gives the integration-by-parts identity.
Choose u and dv so the remaining integral is simpler; include the integration constant.
For a nonnegative probability density p on its full domain, what must its integral equal?
The total probability over all possible values is one. The density itself can exceed one over a short interval.
Arc length for a continuously differentiable graph y = f(x) on [a,b].
In Euler’s method, which slope advances the current point?
The slope at the next, unknown point.
The average of all prior slopes.
The slope zero in every step.
Forward Euler uses the known current slope and step size h to estimate the next value.
yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f(xₙ,yₙ); xₙ₊₁ = xₙ + h
Approximation for y′ = f(x,y); smaller h often improves accuracy but stability still matters.
For x = x(t), y = y(t), how is dy/dx computed when x′(t) ≠ 0?
Both derivatives are with respect to t. Dividing eliminates the common parameter change.
The slope formula requires dx/dt ≠ 0. The polar area formula assumes the region is swept once.
If aₙ does not approach zero, what can you conclude about Σaₙ?
A necessary condition for convergence is aₙ → 0. That condition alone is not sufficient.
The geometric-series sum applies only when the common ratio has magnitude below one.
What is the dot product of two nonzero perpendicular vectors?
The dot product is |a||b| cos θ, and cos 90° = 0.
a · b = |a||b| cos θ; |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ
Dot product is scalar; cross product in three dimensions is a vector oriented by the right-hand rule.
If r(t) is position, which vector gives acceleration?
Velocity is the first time derivative of position. Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
Speed is scalar; velocity and acceleration are vectors.
When finding ∂f/∂x for f(x,y), how is y treated?
As a function of x in every case.
A partial derivative varies one independent variable while holding the others fixed.
The directional vector must be a unit vector and f must be differentiable at the point.
Which area element is used in polar coordinates?
The Jacobian factor r accounts for the growing arc length of an angular strip as radius increases.
dA = r dr dθ; dV = ρ² sin φ dρ dφ dθ
For spherical coordinates here, φ is measured from the positive z-axis.
For a conservative field F = ∇f, what determines the line integral from A to B?
The fundamental theorem for line integrals makes the integral depend only on the endpoint potential difference.
Assume f has continuous first partial derivatives along a piecewise smooth path in its domain.
For y″ + ω²y = 0 with ω > 0, which family is the general solution?
Differentiating sine or cosine twice multiplies it by −ω², which makes y″ + ω²y equal zero.
ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 ⇒ ar² + br + c = 0
For constant coefficients and a ≠ 0; repeated and complex characteristic roots require their corresponding solution forms.
physics: When adding measured lengths, what must you do first?
Addition requires the same physical dimension and compatible units. Convert before combining values.
Track units through each conversion; dimensionless conversion ratios equal one.
Can an object have zero velocity at an instant and nonzero acceleration?
Yes, such as at the top of a vertical toss.
No, acceleration must then be zero.
Only if its mass is zero.
At the top of an ideal vertical toss, instantaneous velocity is zero while gravitational acceleration remains downward.
v = v₀ + at; x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at²
These kinematic equations require constant acceleration.
For a vector at angle θ from +x, what is its x component?
The adjacent projection on the x-axis is magnitude times cosine of the angle measured from +x.
Aₓ = A cos θ; Aᵧ = A sin θ
Use the stated angle convention and retain the signs of the components.
Motion in two and three dimensions
Without air resistance, what is a projectile’s horizontal acceleration?
In the ideal projectile model gravity acts vertically, so horizontal velocity remains constant.
x = x₀ + v₀ₓt; y = y₀ + v₀ᵧt − ½gt²
Flat-Earth model, constant g, upward +y, and no air resistance.
An object moves at constant velocity. What is its net force in an inertial frame?
Constant velocity means zero acceleration. Newton’s second law then gives zero net force.
Constant-mass particle in an inertial frame; apply the vector equation component by component.
Which statement about static friction is accurate?
It adjusts up to a maximum μₛN.
It always points in the direction of motion.
It is independent of contact forces.
Static friction adjusts to prevent slipping until the required magnitude exceeds μₛN.
The kinetic-friction relation is the ideal sliding model. Centripetal acceleration points toward the curvature center.
A force always perpendicular to an object’s displacement does how much work?
The work element is F · dr. Perpendicular vectors have zero dot product.
Classical particle kinetic energy; net work includes all forces.
When only conservative forces do work, which quantity is constant?
Conservative forces exchange kinetic and potential energy while their sum remains constant.
With nonconservative work, use Δ(K + U) = Wnonconservative.
When is the total momentum of a system conserved?
When net external force is zero.
Internal forces cancel in the system momentum balance. Zero net external force gives constant total momentum.
Vector quantities; for a system use net external force and total momentum.
Two points on the same rigid rotating disk share which quantity?
Arc length traveled at different radii.
Rigid-body rotation gives all points the same angular velocity. Their tangential speeds depend on radius.
v = rω; aₜ = rα; aᵣ = rω²
For rotation about a fixed axis; r is perpendicular distance from that axis.
For pure rolling on a stationary surface, which relation holds?
The no-slip contact constraint makes translational speed of the center equal R times angular speed.
Use the same reference point and an appropriate inertial origin for the torque–angular momentum relation.
What must hold for a rigid body in static equilibrium?
Both net force and net torque are zero.
Zero net force prevents translational acceleration; zero net torque prevents angular acceleration.
The elastic relation assumes small deformation within the material’s linear elastic range.
If separation between two point masses doubles, their gravitational attraction becomes what fraction?
Point masses or spherically symmetric bodies outside their surfaces; potential is zero at infinity.
For a static fluid of constant density, how does pressure change with depth?
It increases by ρg times the depth increase.
It depends only on container width.
The weight of the overlying fluid gives Δp = ρgΔh for a constant-density fluid.
p = p₀ + ρgh; FB = ρfluid gVdisplaced
Hydrostatic model with constant density and gravitational acceleration.
In simple harmonic motion, acceleration is proportional to what?
The restoring acceleration points toward equilibrium and has magnitude proportional to displacement.
Ideal linear spring and negligible damping for the spring formula.
Does a traveling wave generally require the medium to travel along with the wave?
Yes, every particle follows the crest.
No, particles oscillate while the disturbance travels.
A mechanical wave transports a disturbance and energy. Individual medium particles can oscillate about equilibrium.
Ideal taut string with small transverse displacement and uniform linear density μ.
For a point source radiating uniformly, how does intensity change when distance doubles?
The same power spreads over an area 4πr², so doubling r reduces intensity by four.
Uniform spherical spreading without absorption; sound level β is in decibels.
Thermal equilibrium between two bodies implies equality of what?
Thermal equilibrium means no net heat transfer caused by a temperature difference.
Use mcΔT within one phase with appropriate specific heat; mL describes a phase change.
For an ideal gas, average translational kinetic energy per molecule depends on what?
The mean translational kinetic energy is 3kBT/2, determined by absolute temperature.
For an isolated system, total entropy can do what?
The second law gives ΔS ≥ 0 for an isolated system, with equality for a reversible process.
Compute entropy along a reversible path; reservoir temperatures must be in kelvins.
Two positive point charges exert what kind of electric force on one another?
Like charges repel along the line joining the charges; unlike charges attract.
Point charges in vacuum; include directions when adding forces.
How is electric field related to the force on a positive test charge?
Electric field is force per unit positive test charge and points in the direction of that force.
Test-charge limit; superpose vector fields from multiple charges.
Electric flux through a closed surface depends on which charge?
Only charges exactly on the surface.
Gauss’s law relates net outward flux to net charge enclosed, even though outside charges may affect the local field.
Closed surface with outward area vectors; symmetry is needed to easily solve for E.
Moving a charge q through potential difference ΔV changes its potential energy by what?
Potential difference is potential-energy change per unit charge, so ΔU = qΔV.
Electrostatics; electric potential is scalar and its reference zero is arbitrary.
For a fixed ideal capacitor, doubling applied voltage does what to stored charge magnitude?
Q = CV and C is fixed in this ideal model, so charge is proportional to voltage.
Linear capacitor with fixed geometry and dielectric response.
Electric current is the rate of change of which quantity through a cross-section?
Current is charge flow per unit time, I = dQ/dt.
I = dQ/dt; V = IR; R = ρL/A
V = IR assumes ohmic behavior at the stated physical conditions.
Kirchhoff’s junction rule follows from conservation of what?
Charge does not accumulate at an ideal steady-state junction, so total incoming current equals outgoing current.
Use consistent signs; the simple loop rule assumes no unaccounted changing magnetic flux.
A charge moving parallel to a magnetic field experiences what magnetic force?
qvB in the direction of motion.
The magnetic force qv × B is zero for parallel or antiparallel velocity and field.
This is the magnetic contribution; add qE if an electric field is also present.
Around a long straight wire, the magnetic field direction is what?
Tangent to circles around the wire.
The right-hand rule gives circular field lines around the current direction.
Long straight wire in vacuum, at perpendicular distance r outside the wire.
Lenz’s law fixes an induced current’s direction so that its magnetic effect does what?
Opposes the change in magnetic flux.
The induced effect opposes the change in flux that produces it, consistent with energy conservation.
N identical coil turns; orient the loop normal and positive circulation consistently.
An ideal LC circuit repeatedly exchanges energy between which stores?
Energy oscillates between the capacitor’s electric field and the inductor’s magnetic field.
Ideal LC oscillation neglects resistance and energy loss.
What does zero net magnetic flux through a closed surface express?
Magnetic poles occur only as isolated north poles.
No isolated magnetic monopoles in classical Maxwell theory.
Gauss’s law for magnetism gives zero net flux through a closed surface; magnetic field lines form continuous loops.
Integral Maxwell equations in vacuum with consistently oriented surfaces and paths.
In a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum, E and B are oriented how?
Parallel to each other and propagation.
Perpendicular to each other and propagation.
A vacuum plane electromagnetic wave is transverse: E, B, and propagation form mutually perpendicular directions.
Plane traveling electromagnetic wave in vacuum.
For a plane mirror, the image lies where?
Twice the object distance in front.
The same distance behind as the object is in front.
Reflected rays appear to come from a virtual image equally far behind the plane mirror.
Paraxial thin-lens or spherical-mirror equation with the book’s corresponding sign convention; plane mirror i = −p.
Two coherent waves arriving in phase tend to produce what?
In-phase displacements add. Equal in-phase waves double amplitude and give four times one wave’s intensity.
Double slit: d sin θ = mλ
Bright fringes for coherent, in-phase illumination of narrow slits; m is an integer.
Making a single slit narrower generally does what to its central diffraction maximum?
The first minimum satisfies a sin θ = λ, so decreasing slit width a increases the angular spread.
Single slit: a sin θ = mλ, m = ±1, ±2, …
Fraunhofer single-slit minima; the formula does not describe the central maximum at m = 0.
Which speed is the same for all inertial observers in special relativity?
A sound wave’s speed in air.
The invariance of vacuum light speed is a postulate of special relativity.
Δτ is proper time between events occurring at one position in the clock’s rest frame.
Increasing a photon’s frequency increases what?
Photon energy is hf. Its vacuum speed stays c and its wavelength decreases as frequency increases.
For a photon use its vacuum wavelength; the de Broglie relation uses particle momentum.
What is the physical meaning of |ψ|² for a normalized one-particle wavefunction?
The squared magnitude gives probability per unit configuration-space volume. Its full-space integral is one.
Energy formula for a nonrelativistic particle in a one-dimensional infinite well of width L, n = 1,2,…
In the simple hydrogen model, atomic energy levels are what?
Bound hydrogen states occupy discrete energies labeled by integer principal quantum number n.
Nonrelativistic hydrogen approximation, neglecting fine structure and reduced-mass corrections.
What is the defining band feature of an intrinsic semiconductor?
A small gap between valence and conduction bands.
A perfectly filled conduction band at all temperatures.
A relatively small band gap permits thermally excited electrons in the conduction band and holes in the valence band.
Simple electron-and-hole transport model with carrier densities n and mobilities μ.
After one half-life, what fraction of a large radioactive sample’s parent nuclei remains on average?
Half-life is the time for the expected parent-nucleus population to decrease by a factor of two.
N(t) = N₀e⁻λt; T½ = ln 2/λ; A = λN
Constant decay probability; predictions describe the statistical population.
Energy released in a nuclear reaction corresponds to what?
An increase in total rest mass only.
A decrease in total rest mass.
A change in electric charge conservation.
A lower final rest mass leaves energy available as particle kinetic energy or radiation while total energy is conserved.
Use consistent nuclear or atomic mass accounting and include all reaction products.
Quarks, leptons, and the Big Bang
In the quark model, a proton contains which valence quarks?
Two up quarks and one down quark have total charge 2/3 + 2/3 − 1/3 = +1 in elementary-charge units.
These are quark electric charges; composite-particle charge is the sum of constituent charges.
chemistry: Essential Ideas
Which observation provides evidence that a chemical change has occurred?
A new substance with different chemical properties forms.
A sample is cut into smaller pieces.
A liquid changes shape to fit its container.
A solid is measured on a balance.
A chemical change changes chemical identity. Cutting, changing container shape, and measuring mass can occur without forming a new substance.
ρ = m/V

ρ is density, m is sample mass, and V is its volume. Use compatible units: SI density is kg/m³; laboratory densities often use g/mL. The measured sample and its temperature must match the stated density.
Atoms, Molecules, and Ions
What distinguishes two isotopes of the same element?
They have different numbers of protons.
They have different numbers of neutrons.
They must have opposite electrical charges.
They have different atomic numbers.
Isotopes share the same atomic number and therefore the same proton count, but differ in neutron count and mass number. Changing electrons instead creates ions.
A = Z + N; q/e = Z − Nₑ

A is mass number, Z is proton count (atomic number), N is neutron count, and Nₑ is electron count. q is the atom or ion charge; e is the positive elementary charge. These are particle counts, so A is not the element’s average atomic mass.
Electronic Structure and Periodic Properties of Elements
For a photon traveling in vacuum, what happens to its energy when its wavelength increases?
Its energy increases because the wave is longer.
Its energy stays fixed for every photon.
Its energy decreases because energy is inversely proportional to wavelength.
Its energy becomes negative.
Photon energy is E = hc/λ. With h and c fixed, a larger wavelength gives a smaller positive energy and a lower frequency.
E = hν = hc/λ
E is photon energy in J, h = 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, ν is frequency in s⁻¹, c = 2.99792458 × 10⁸ m/s, and λ is vacuum wavelength in m. Use vacuum c; convert nm to m before calculating.
Chemical Bonding and Molecular Geometry
A central atom has four electron domains: two bonds and two lone pairs. What molecular shape does VSEPR predict?
Linear.
Trigonal planar.
Tetrahedral molecular shape.
Bent molecular shape.
Four electron domains have a tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement. Molecular shape describes only the bonded atoms, so two bonds plus two lone pairs give a bent shape.
FC = V − L − B/2

FC is formal charge in elementary-charge units, V is the neutral atom’s valence-electron count, L is its nonbonding-electron count, and B is its bonding-electron count. Count every lone-pair electron and split bonding electrons equally. Formal charge is bookkeeping, not a measured partial charge.
Advanced Theories of Bonding
According to molecular orbital theory, what makes a molecule paramagnetic?
At least one occupied molecular orbital contains an unpaired electron.
Every electron is paired in an occupied orbital.
The molecule has no antibonding orbitals.
The molecule’s bond order must equal zero.

Unpaired electrons make a species paramagnetic. A species whose electrons are all paired is diamagnetic; bonding and antibonding occupation alone does not settle this without examining electron pairing.
Bond order = (N_bonding − N_antibonding)/2

N_bonding and N_antibonding count electrons in bonding and antibonding molecular orbitals in the chosen MO diagram. Fill the appropriate diagram using Aufbau, Pauli, and Hund rules. This MO bond order is a model of net bonding; zero does not predict a stable ordinary covalent bond.
Composition of Substances and Solutions
When calculating molarity, which volume belongs in the denominator?
The volume of solute alone.
The final volume of the complete solution.
The solvent volume before the solute is added in every case.
The volume of the measuring flask’s glass.
Molarity is moles of solute divided by total solution volume. Adding solute can change volume, so the solvent’s original volume is not automatically the final solution volume.
c = n_solute/V_solution; n = m/M_m

c is molarity in mol/L, n is amount in mol, V_solution is final solution volume in L, m is solute mass in g, and M_m is molar mass in g/mol. Convert mL to L. Molarity depends on temperature because solution volume can change.
Stoichiometry of Chemical Reactions
What do the coefficients in a balanced chemical equation tell you for a mole-to-mole conversion?
The masses of reactants must be equal.
The molar masses of reactants and products are equal.
The relative amounts in moles that react or form.
The reaction must go completely in both directions at once.
Balanced coefficients give stoichiometric mole ratios, not mass ratios. To convert a mass, first use molar mass to find moles, then apply the balanced coefficient ratio.
n_B = (b/a)n_A

a and b are the balanced coefficients of consumed A and formed B; n_A is the amount of A that actually reacts, and n_B is the stoichiometric amount of B formed. For theoretical yield, use the limiting reactant and assume the stated reaction proceeds completely without side reactions. Excess reactant does not determine the yield.
Gases
Why must temperature be expressed in kelvin in the ideal gas law?
Kelvin and Celsius have identical zero points.
Kelvin values remove the need to choose pressure units.
The gas constant is only defined for temperatures below freezing.
The law uses absolute temperature, whose zero represents the absolute thermal scale.
Gas-law proportionalities use absolute temperature. Celsius has an arbitrary offset, so doubling a Celsius reading does not double absolute temperature. Convert using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
PV = nRT

P is absolute pressure, V is gas volume, n is amount in mol, T is temperature in K, and R = 8.314462618 J/(mol·K) for P in Pa and V in m³. Alternatively use R = 0.082057 L·atm/(mol·K) with L and atm. The ideal approximation works best at relatively low pressure and high temperature, away from condensation.
Thermochemistry
If a reaction releases heat to its surroundings at constant pressure, what is the sign of the reaction’s enthalpy change?
Negative: the reacting system loses heat.
Positive: the surroundings become warmer.
Always zero because energy is conserved.
Its sign is determined only by the reaction speed.
An exothermic reaction transfers heat out of the reacting system, so its ΔH is negative at constant pressure. The surroundings gain heat; system and surroundings have opposite heat-transfer signs.
q = mcΔT; q_p = ΔH

q is heat transferred into the chosen sample, m is mass, c is specific heat capacity, and ΔT = T_final − T_initial. With m in g and c in J/(g·K), q is in J. Treat c as constant over the range and exclude phase changes. q_p = ΔH applies at constant pressure with only pressure–volume work; distinguish the reaction system from calorimeter surroundings.
Liquids and Solids
Why does a liquid boil when its vapor pressure equals the external pressure?
All intermolecular attractions have permanently disappeared.
Vapor bubbles can persist and grow throughout the liquid.
Its molecules stop moving.
The liquid must be at its critical temperature.
At the boiling point, vapor pressure balances the external pressure, allowing vapor bubbles to exist inside the liquid. Lowering external pressure lowers the boiling temperature.
ln(P₂/P₁) = −(ΔH_vap/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁)

P₁ and P₂ are equilibrium vapor pressures of the same substance; T₁ and T₂ are absolute temperatures in K. ΔH_vap is molar enthalpy of vaporization in J/mol and R = 8.314462618 J/(mol·K). ln is the natural logarithm. This integrated Clausius–Clapeyron approximation assumes ideal vapor, negligible liquid volume, and nearly constant ΔH_vap over the temperature interval.
Solutions and Colloids
For ideal dilute solutions with the same solvent, what primarily determines the size of a colligative effect?
The color of the dissolved solute.
The shape of the container.
The number of dissolved solute particles relative to the solvent amount.
Only the mass of one solute molecule.

Colligative properties depend on the amount of dissolved particles rather than their chemical identity in the ideal dilute limit. Dissociation can increase particle count, so equal formula-unit concentrations need not give equal effects.
ΔT_f = iK_f b

ΔT_f = T_freezing,pure − T_freezing,solution is a positive freezing-point depression, i is the effective van ’t Hoff factor, K_f is the solvent’s freezing-point constant in K·kg/mol, and b is solute molality in mol/kg of solvent. Use solvent mass, not solution volume. This is a dilute-solution approximation; ion interactions can make i differ from the ideal dissociation count.
Thermodynamics
At fixed temperature and pressure, what does ΔG < 0 tell you about the stated process?
It must happen instantaneously.
It must release heat in every case.
It cannot proceed spontaneously.
It is thermodynamically spontaneous in the stated direction under those conditions.

A negative Gibbs free energy change indicates a spontaneous direction at fixed temperature and pressure. It does not predict reaction speed; an activation barrier can make a spontaneous reaction very slow.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS

ΔG is Gibbs free energy change, ΔH is enthalpy change, ΔS is entropy change, and T is absolute temperature in K. Use consistent energy units: convert ΔS from J/(mol·K) if ΔH is in kJ/mol. The simple finite-change expression assumes the initial and final states are at the same temperature; the spontaneity criterion applies at fixed T and P with only pressure–volume work.
Fundamental Equilibrium Concepts
What is true when a reversible chemical reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium?
The forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, though reactions continue.
Both reactions stop permanently.
Every reactant concentration equals every product concentration.
The equilibrium constant becomes zero.
Dynamic equilibrium means equal forward and reverse rates. Concentrations remain constant, but their values need not be equal, and molecular-scale reactions continue.

For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, a, b, c, d are balanced stoichiometric coefficients and bracketed terms are equilibrium molar concentrations. Omit pure solids and pure liquids. K_c belongs to the written reaction at a specified temperature; reverse the reaction to obtain its reciprocal. Concentration expressions are the introductory approximation to dimensionless activity-based equilibrium constants.
Acid-Base Equilibria
Which statement describes a Brønsted–Lowry conjugate acid–base pair?
The two species differ by one electron.
The two species differ by one proton, H⁺.
They must have equal electrical charges.
They must both contain hydroxide ions.
An acid becomes its conjugate base by donating one proton, and a base becomes its conjugate acid by accepting one proton. An acid–base conjugate pair differs by exactly H⁺, not by an electron.
pH = −log₁₀ a(H₃O⁺) ≈ −log₁₀([H₃O⁺]/(1 mol/L))

a(H₃O⁺) is the dimensionless hydronium activity. In a sufficiently dilute aqueous solution, approximate it by molar concentration divided by the standard concentration 1 mol/L. log₁₀ is base ten. Neutrality means [H₃O⁺] = [OH⁻]; neutral pH is 7.00 at 25 °C and changes when the water ionization constant changes with temperature.
Equilibria of Other Reaction Classes
For a dilute AgCl solution at a fixed temperature, what does Q_sp > K_sp predict?
More AgCl must dissolve until all solid disappears.
No phase change is possible.
AgCl precipitation is thermodynamically favored until equilibrium is restored.
The value of K_sp permanently increases.

Q_sp is the current ion product. If it exceeds K_sp, the solution is supersaturated with respect to AgCl and precipitation lowers dissolved ion concentrations toward equilibrium. K_sp stays fixed at the same temperature.
AgCl(s) ⇌ Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); K_sp ≈ [Ag⁺][Cl⁻]

The dissolution has a 1:1 ion ratio. Brackets denote equilibrium molar concentrations in the dilute approximation; the exact thermodynamic expression uses dimensionless activities. Pure solid AgCl is omitted because its activity is one. Q_sp uses current concentrations and K_sp uses equilibrium values at the given temperature; do not use K_sp = s² when a common ion or other equilibrium changes the ion concentrations.
Electrochemistry
Where does oxidation occur in an electrochemical cell?
At the cathode in every cell.
Only inside the salt bridge.
At whichever electrode has the larger physical area.
At the anode in both galvanic and electrolytic cells.

Oxidation is electron loss and always occurs at the anode; reduction occurs at the cathode. Electrode signs differ between galvanic and electrolytic cells, so naming the process is more reliable than memorizing a sign alone.
E°_cell = E°_cathode − E°_anode; ΔG° = −nFE°_cell

Use standard reduction potentials for both electrodes, subtracting anode from cathode. E° is in V; n is moles of electrons transferred per mole of the balanced cell reaction, and F = 96485.33212 C/mol. ΔG° is in J/mol of reaction. Standard conditions use unit activities and the table’s temperature. Never multiply electrode potentials by balancing coefficients; only n scales when the reaction is multiplied.
Kinetics
Can the reaction orders in a general experimentally measured rate law always be read from the overall balanced equation?
No; overall reaction orders generally must be determined experimentally.
Yes; every exponent always equals its balanced coefficient.
Yes; every reactant always has first order.
No; reaction orders can never be determined.
The overall balanced equation gives stoichiometry, but generally does not specify the rate law. Orders come from experiment unless a known elementary step justifies using its reactant coefficients.
rate = k[A]^m[B]^n

k is the rate constant at the specified temperature, [A] and [B] are reactant molar concentrations, and m and n are experimental reaction orders. For rate in mol/(L·s), units of k are (mol/L)^(1−m−n)/s. Orders may be zero, fractional, or negative. Do not equate orders with overall stoichiometric coefficients without a justified elementary-step model.
Representative Metals, Metalloids, and Nonmetals
When a carbonate ion reacts with enough aqueous acid, which gas is formed?
Hydrogen, H₂.
Carbon dioxide, CO₂.
Nitrogen, N₂.
Chlorine, Cl₂.
Acid protonates carbonate to form carbonic acid, which yields water and carbon dioxide. The net ionic equation consumes two H⁺ per carbonate ion and conserves both atoms and charge.
CO₃²⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq) → CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

This is a balanced net ionic reaction for carbonate under acidic aqueous conditions; spectator ions are omitted. One mole of carbonate consumes two moles of H⁺ and can form one mole of CO₂ with sufficient acid. CO₃²⁻ has −2 charge, so the total charge is zero on both sides. Bicarbonate, HCO₃⁻, instead requires one H⁺ per ion.
Transition Metals and Coordination Chemistry
A metal is bonded to six monodentate NH₃ ligands. What is its coordination number?
Three because NH₃ contains three hydrogens.
Zero because NH₃ is electrically neutral.
Six because six ligand donor atoms bond to the metal.
The same number as the metal’s oxidation state in every case.

Coordination number counts donor atoms directly bonded to the central metal. Each monodentate NH₃ supplies one donor nitrogen, so six NH₃ ligands provide six donor atoms. Coordination number and oxidation state are different quantities.
q_complex = z_metal + Σq_ligands

q_complex is the complex ion’s net charge, z_metal is the metal oxidation state, and Σq_ligands is the sum of all ligand charges, counting each occurrence. Use elementary-charge units. Neutral NH₃ and H₂O each contribute zero; Cl⁻ contributes −1. Charge bookkeeping determines oxidation state, not coordination number or high-spin versus low-spin electron arrangement.
Nuclear Chemistry
For a fixed radionuclide undergoing ordinary first-order radioactive decay, what happens to its half-life when the initial sample contains more nuclei?
It doubles whenever the sample doubles.
It becomes zero for large samples.
It is determined by the sample’s chemical color.
It remains the same; only the initial activity increases.

The decay constant and half-life are properties of the radionuclide under ordinary conditions. A larger number of undecayed nuclei gives higher initial activity, but the same fraction decays during one half-life.
N(t) = N₀e^(−λt); t₁/₂ = ln(2)/λ

N(t) is the number of undecayed parent nuclei at time t, N₀ is its initial value, λ is the positive decay constant, and ln is the natural logarithm. Use the same time units for t and 1/λ. This single-parent exponential assumes no replenishment of that parent and no mixture of different decay constants; daughter ingrowth needs additional equations.
Organic Chemistry
Which structural feature distinguishes an alkene from an alkane?
At least one carbon–carbon double bond.
An oxygen atom in every molecule.
A nitrogen atom in every molecule.
Only carbon–carbon single bonds and no multiple bonds.

An alkene contains a carbon–carbon double bond. Alkanes are saturated hydrocarbons with only single bonds. Carbon rings and oxygen- or nitrogen-containing functional groups require additional structural classification.
CₙH₂ₙ₊₂

This molecular formula applies to a neutral acyclic saturated hydrocarbon (an alkane) with n ≥ 1 carbon atoms and no heteroatoms. It does not apply unchanged to rings or multiple bonds: one ring or one double bond reduces hydrogen count by two relative to the acyclic alkane. A formula alone does not identify connectivity.
organic: Structure and Bonding
How many σ and π bonds form a carbon–carbon triple bond?
One σ bond and two π bonds.
Three σ bonds.
Two σ bonds and one π bond.
Three π bonds.
The sp orbitals form the σ bond; two pairs of unhybridized p orbitals form the two π bonds.
C≡C: 1 σ + 2 π; carbon is sp-hybridized.
For an ordinary carbon–carbon triple bond; its bond axes are approximately linear. Reference: chapter 1 Summary, PDF p. 47 (printed p. 29).
Polar Covalent Bonds; Acids and Bases
Within the same solvent, which acid is strongest?
The acid with the largest pKa.
The acid with the smallest pKa.
The acid with the smallest Ka.
All acids have identical strength.
A smaller pKa means a larger acid-dissociation constant and greater tendency to donate a proton.
pKa = −log₁₀Ka
Compare values determined under comparable solvent and temperature conditions. Reference: chapter 2 Summary, PDF p. 80 (printed p. 62).
Organic Compounds: Alkanes and Their Stereochemistry
Which statement describes constitutional isomers?
Same connectivity, different bond rotation only.
Different molecular formulas, same mass.
Same molecular formula, different atom connectivity.
Mirror images with identical connectivity.
Constitutional isomers differ in the connections between atoms; conformers differ only by rotations.
Acyclic saturated alkane: CₙH₂ₙ₊₂
The alkane formula assumes an open-chain hydrocarbon with no rings or multiple bonds. Reference: chapter 3 Summary, PDF p. 116 (printed p. 98).
Organic Compounds: Cycloalkanes and Their Stereochemistry
Why does methylcyclohexane favor an equatorial methyl group?
It changes the molecular formula.
It removes all carbon–carbon bonds.
It forces the ring into a planar hexagon.
It reduces 1,3-diaxial steric interactions.
An axial methyl group crowds axial hydrogens on carbons three positions away; equatorial placement reduces that crowding.
Chair flip: axial ⇄ equatorial; up/down orientation is retained.
Apply to cyclohexane chairs; a ring flip changes conformation, not cis/trans configuration. Reference: chapter 4 Summary, PDF p. 145 (printed p. 127).
Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
What defines a pair of enantiomers?
Nonsuperimposable mirror-image stereoisomers.
Isomers differing only in connectivity.
Any two conformers of one molecule.
Any two molecules with different formulas.
Enantiomers share connectivity but are mirror images that cannot be superimposed.
Maximum configurations from n independent stereocenters: 2ⁿ
The actual count can be smaller because of symmetry, including meso forms; R/S does not predict rotation sign. Reference: chapter 5 Summary, PDF p. 180 (printed p. 162).
An Overview of Organic Reactions
In a polar reaction, what does an ordinary double-barbed curved arrow track?
Movement of an atomic nucleus.
Movement of an electron pair.
Movement of a single electron only.
The path of an entire solvent molecule.
A double-barbed arrow starts at an electron pair or bond and points to its destination; a fishhook tracks one electron.
Nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electrophile.
Use double-barbed arrows for polar mechanisms and fishhooks for single-electron radical steps. Reference: chapter 6 Summary, PDF p. 216 (printed p. 198).
Alkenes: Structure and Reactivity
During ionic addition of HBr to propene, why is 2-bromopropane the major product?
Bromide first removes every hydrogen.
A primary carbocation is always more stable.
Protonation favors the more stable secondary carbocation.
The double bond remains unchanged.
Protonation that gives the secondary carbocation is favored; bromide then bonds at that carbon.
Markovnikov addition: H adds to the carbon bearing more H atoms.
For the ordinary ionic HBr mechanism without peroxide-driven radical conditions; rearrangements can matter for other substrates. Reference: chapter 7 Summary, PDF p. 252 (printed p. 234).
Alkenes: Reactions and Synthesis
What alcohol forms from hydroboration–oxidation of propene?
2-Propanol.
Propanone.
Propanoic acid.
1-Propanol.
Hydroboration places boron at the less substituted carbon; oxidation replaces C–B with C–OH.
Alkene → alcohol: 1. BH₃; 2. H₂O₂, OH⁻
Net non-Markovnikov hydration with syn addition; use the sequential reagents shown. Reference: chapter 8 Summary, PDF p. 293 (printed p. 275).
Alkynes: An Introduction to Organic Synthesis
Partial hydrogenation of an internal alkyne with Lindlar catalyst gives which product?
A cis alkene.
A trans alkene as the sole product.
A ketone.
A carboxylic acid.
The poisoned catalyst allows syn addition of hydrogen and stops at the alkene stage.
Internal alkyne + H₂/Lindlar → cis alkene
Contrast dissolving-metal reduction, which favors trans alkenes; terminal alkene products have no cis/trans pair. Reference: chapter 9 Summary, PDF p. 323 (printed p. 305).
Organohalides
Why must Grignard reagents be kept away from water?
Water makes the C–Mg bond permanent.
Water protonates and destroys the reagent.
Water converts every reagent to benzene.
Water prevents any acid–base reaction.
The carbon bonded to magnesium is strongly basic and reacts with a proton donor to produce a hydrocarbon.
RMgX + H₂O → RH + Mg(OH)X
Prepare and use Grignard reagents in dry ether; avoid acidic O–H or N–H groups before workup. Reference: chapter 10 Summary, PDF p. 350 (printed p. 332).
Reactions of Alkyl Halides: Nucleophilic Substitutions and Eliminations
What stereochemical change occurs at a reacting stereocenter in an SN2 substitution?
Guaranteed retention from frontside attack.
Complete carbocation equilibration.
Inversion of configuration from backside attack.
Loss of all stereocenters in the molecule.
The nucleophile attacks opposite the leaving group, causing geometrical inversion at the reacting carbon.
SN2 rate = k[substrate][nucleophile]
For a concerted SN2 step; an R label need not become S if substituent priority order changes. Reference: chapter 11 Summary, PDF p. 390 (printed p. 372).
Structure Determination: Mass Spectrometry and Infrared Spectroscopy
What do infrared absorption bands primarily report about an organic molecule?
The exact number of all stereocenters.
Its proton NMR integration.
Its chromosome sequence.
Its bond vibrations and functional groups.
IR absorption occurs when radiation excites appropriate stretching or bending vibrations.
IR wavenumber: ν̃ = 1/λ; units cm⁻¹
Band positions depend on bond type and environment; IR-active vibrations change dipole moment. Use multiple bands together. Reference: chapter 12 Summary, PDF p. 427 (printed p. 409).
Structure Determination: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
A proton coupled to two equivalent neighboring protons in a simple first-order spectrum usually gives what pattern?
A triplet.
A singlet.
A doublet.
A quartet.
For n equivalent coupled neighbors, the first-order n + 1 rule gives three lines when n = 2.
First-order splitting: n equivalent neighbors → n + 1 lines

The simple rule assumes suitable first-order coupling; exchangeable protons, nonequivalent neighbors and strong coupling can behave differently. Reference: chapter 13 Summary, PDF p. 461 (printed p. 443).
Conjugated Compounds and Ultraviolet Spectroscopy
Which diene conformation is needed for a standard Diels–Alder cycloaddition?
s-Trans locked so it cannot rotate.
s-Cis.
A saturated chain with no π bonds.
A diene with no conjugation.
The s-cis arrangement places the conjugated diene ends close enough to form the two new σ bonds.
Conjugated diene + dienophile → cyclohexene framework
The diene must be able to adopt s-cis; the usual thermal [4+2] reaction is concerted and stereospecific. Reference: chapter 14 Summary, PDF p. 496 (printed p. 478).
Benzene and Aromaticity
Which π-electron count can satisfy the Hückel rule for a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring?
Four π electrons.
Eight π electrons.
Six π electrons.
Twelve π electrons.
Six satisfies 4n + 2 with n = 1. Counting electrons alone is insufficient without the stated geometry and conjugation.
Aromatic monocyclic π system: 4n + 2 electrons
Requires cyclic, planar, uninterrupted p-orbital overlap; 4n systems under these conditions are antiaromatic. Reference: chapter 15 Summary, PDF p. 527 (printed p. 509).
Chemistry of Benzene: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution
How does chlorine on chlorobenzene affect electrophilic aromatic substitution?
It activates the ring and directs only meta.
It deactivates the ring and directs only meta.
It removes the need for an electrophile.
It deactivates the ring but directs ortho/para.
Its inductive withdrawal deactivates the ring, while lone-pair resonance donation favors ortho and para attack.
Halogens: deactivating, ortho/para-directing substituents.
For electrophilic aromatic substitution; directing effects differ from nucleophilic aromatic substitution. Reference: chapter 16 Summary, PDF p. 575 (printed p. 557).
Alcohols and Phenols
Which product typically forms when a secondary alcohol is oxidized without C–C bond cleavage?
A ketone.
An aldehyde.
An ether.
An alkane.
Oxidation removes hydrogen from oxygen and the hydroxyl-bearing carbon to form a carbonyl.
R₂CHOH → R₂C=O
For ordinary secondary-alcohol oxidation; tertiary alcohols lack the necessary hydrogen and resist analogous oxidation. Reference: chapter 17 Summary, PDF p. 620 (printed p. 602).
Ethers and Epoxides; Thiols and Sulfides
Where does a strong nucleophile generally attack an unsymmetrical epoxide under basic conditions?
Always at the more substituted carbon.
At the less hindered epoxide carbon.
Only at the oxygen atom.
Only at a remote methyl group.
Basic ring opening follows an SN2-like attack at the less crowded carbon, breaking that carbon–oxygen bond.
Epoxide + Nu⁻ → ring-opened alkoxide → alcohol after workup
For nucleophilic opening under basic conditions; acid-catalyzed regiochemistry requires a separate analysis. Reference: chapter 18 Summary, PDF p. 652 (printed p. 634).
Aldehydes and Ketones: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions
After aqueous workup, what does NaBH₄ reduction of an ordinary ketone produce?
An alkene.
A carboxylic acid.
A secondary alcohol.
An amide.
Hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon, and the resulting alkoxide is protonated during workup.
R₂C=O → R₂CHOH
NaBH₄ reduces ordinary aldehydes and ketones; do not assume identical reactivity for all carboxylic acid derivatives. Reference: chapter 19 Summary, PDF p. 710 (printed p. 692).
Carboxylic Acids and Nitriles
Why is acetic acid more acidic than ethanol?
Its conjugate base has no electrons.
Ethanol cannot contain an O–H bond.
Acetic acid is a hydrocarbon.
Its conjugate base is resonance stabilized over two oxygens.
Acetate delocalizes its negative charge over two equivalent oxygens; ethoxide lacks that stabilization.
pH = pKa + log₁₀([A⁻]/[HA])
Henderson–Hasselbalch applies to acid/base equilibrium; the concentration form approximates activities in dilute solutions. Reference: chapter 20 Summary, PDF p. 747 (printed p. 729).
Carboxylic Acid Derivatives: Nucleophilic Acyl Substitution Reactions
What is the key mechanistic sequence in nucleophilic acyl substitution?
Nucleophilic addition, then elimination of a leaving group.
Only rotation about a single bond.
Loss of the carbonyl oxygen with no intermediate.
A mandatory free-radical chain.
Attack gives a tetrahedral intermediate; collapse restores the carbonyl and expels a leaving group.
RCOY + Nu → RCONu + leaving group
Applies to acyl derivatives with suitable leaving groups; compare acid chlorides, esters and amides under matched conditions. Reference: chapter 21 Summary, PDF p. 796 (printed p. 778).
Carbonyl Alpha-Substitution Reactions
Why can an α hydrogen next to a carbonyl be removed more readily than a typical alkane hydrogen?
The resulting ion has no charge.
The resulting enolate is resonance stabilized.
All α carbons are aromatic.
A carbonyl prevents all proton transfer.
The enolate distributes charge between the α carbon and oxygen through resonance.
Carbonyl compound + strong base → enolate + conjugate acid
Enolate formation requires an α hydrogen; kinetic/thermodynamic enolate selection depends on base, temperature and equilibration. Reference: chapter 22 Summary, PDF p. 831 (printed p. 813).
Carbonyl Condensation Reactions
Before dehydration, what functional-group pattern does a simple aldol addition create?
An α-chloro ether.
A nitrile with no oxygen.
A β-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone.
A saturated hydrocarbon.
An enolate attacks another carbonyl, producing an alcohol at the β position relative to the retained carbonyl.
Aldol addition → β-hydroxy carbonyl; dehydration → α,β-unsaturated carbonyl
Distinguish addition from condensation with water loss; aldol donors require suitable α hydrogens. Reference: chapter 23 Summary, PDF p. 866 (printed p. 848).
Amines and Heterocycles
Why is aniline generally less basic than a simple alkylamine?
Aniline contains no nitrogen lone pair.
All aromatic compounds are strong bases.
Alkylamines cannot be protonated.
Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the aromatic ring.
Resonance lowers availability of the aniline lone pair for bonding to a proton.
Amine + H⁺ ⇌ ammonium ion
Compare in the same solvent; ring substituents and solvation also affect basicity. Reference: chapter 24 Summary, PDF p. 912 (printed p. 894).
Biomolecules: Carbohydrates
How do the α and β anomers of a cyclic sugar differ?
In configuration at the anomeric carbon.
In molecular formula.
In the number of carbon atoms.
In every stereocenter simultaneously.
Cyclization of the carbonyl creates an anomeric center; α and β forms differ at this new center.
Open-chain sugar ⇌ cyclic hemiacetal (α or β)
For aldoses forming hemiacetals; ketoses form hemiketals. Do not confuse α/β with D/L classification. Reference: chapter 25 Summary, PDF p. 956 (printed p. 938).
Biomolecules: Amino Acids, Peptides, and Proteins
What linkage joins amino acid residues in a peptide?
A carbon–carbon triple bond.
An amide bond.
An ether bond between side chains.
A glycosidic bond.
A peptide bond links the carboxyl-derived carbonyl of one residue to the amino nitrogen of another.
Peptide linkage: C(=O)–N (amide)
Sequences are conventionally read from N terminus to C terminus; primary structure specifies residue order. Reference: chapter 26 Summary, PDF p. 996 (printed p. 978).
Biomolecules: Lipids
What is a triacylglycerol structurally?
Three glucose units linked by glycosidic bonds.
A peptide with three amino acids.
Glycerol esterified with three fatty acids.
A nucleotide with three bases.
Each glycerol hydroxyl forms an ester with a fatty acid; the fatty acid chains may be saturated or unsaturated.
Triacylglycerol hydrolysis → glycerol + fatty acids
Basic hydrolysis (saponification) gives fatty-acid salts rather than neutral fatty acids until acid workup. Reference: chapter 27 Summary, PDF p. 1034 (printed p. 1016).
Biomolecules: Nucleic Acids
What distinguishes a nucleotide from a nucleoside?
A nucleotide lacks a sugar.
A nucleoside has three peptide bonds.
Only nucleosides contain a base.
A nucleotide includes a phosphate group.
A nucleoside contains a base and sugar; adding phosphate gives a nucleotide.
Nucleoside = base + sugar; nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate
DNA uses 2-deoxyribose and RNA uses ribose; polymer backbones contain 3′–5′ phosphodiester links. Reference: chapter 28 Summary, PDF p. 1059 (printed p. 1041).
The Organic Chemistry of Metabolic Pathways
In ordinary fatty-acid β oxidation, how many carbons are removed per repeating cycle?
Two carbons, released as acetyl-CoA.
One carbon, released as methane.
Three carbons, released as glucose.
Six carbons, released as benzene.
Repeated oxidation and cleavage shorten the acyl chain by a two-carbon acetyl unit.
β oxidation: acyl-CoA chain shortens by C₂ per cycle
For the ordinary cycle; the final cleavage and odd-chain or unsaturated substrates need additional accounting or pathways. Reference: chapter 29 Summary, PDF p. 1110 (printed p. 1092).
Orbitals and Organic Chemistry: Pericyclic Reactions
What best describes a pericyclic reaction?
A mechanism that always forms a free carbocation.
A concerted reorganization through a cyclic transition state.
A reaction requiring a long-lived radical intermediate.
Any acid–base reaction in water.
Bond reorganization occurs in one step, with orbital symmetry governing allowed pathways and stereochemistry.
Thermal 4π electrocyclic ring closure: conrotatory; thermal 6π: disrotatory
For idealized electrocyclic closures; photochemical selection rules reverse these rotational modes. Reference: chapter 30 Summary, PDF p. 1137 (printed p. 1119).
Synthetic Polymers
What is characteristic of an isotactic polymer?
Its substituents are placed randomly.
Its stereochemical pattern alternates regularly.
Its repeat-unit stereocenters follow the same stereochemical pattern.
It contains no covalent backbone bonds.
Isotactic chains have a regular repeated arrangement; syndiotactic chains alternate and atactic chains are irregular.
Isotactic = same pattern; syndiotactic = alternating; atactic = irregular
Tacticity describes stereoregularity in suitable polymers; it is distinct from chain-growth versus step-growth mechanisms. Reference: chapter 31 Summary, PDF p. 1159 (printed p. 1141).
linear-algebra: Systems of Linear Equations and Matrices
What makes a list of numbers a solution of a linear system?
It satisfies every equation at the same time.
It satisfies only the first equation.
All its entries must be positive.
Its entries must add to zero.
Substitute the same values into every equation. A solution must make all equations true.
Ax = b
A contains the coefficients, x is the vector of unknowns, and b contains the right-hand sides. The matrix and vector sizes must be compatible.
Determinants
What does a zero determinant tell you about a square matrix?
It is not invertible.
It is always the identity matrix.
Every entry is zero.
Its inverse has determinant one.
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero. Zero determinant means at least one direction is collapsed.
det(A) = ad − bc
For a 2 by 2 matrix with first row (a,b) and second row (c,d). A is invertible exactly when ad − bc is not zero.
Euclidean Vector Spaces
What does a zero dot product mean for two nonzero vectors?
They are perpendicular.
They point in the same direction.
They have equal lengths.
They must be parallel.
The dot product is the product of the lengths and the cosine of the angle. A zero cosine gives a right angle.
u · v = ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ
The angle formula requires both vectors to be nonzero. In standard coordinates, add the products of corresponding components.
General Vector Spaces
What must a basis do?
Span the space and be linearly independent.
Contain every vector in the space.
Contain the zero vector.
Have more vectors than the dimension.
Spanning ensures every vector can be formed. Independence ensures no basis vector is redundant, so coordinates are unique.
v = c₁b₁ + c₂b₂ + ⋯ + cₙbₙ
For a basis b₁,…,bₙ, each vector v has one unique list of coordinates c₁,…,cₙ.
Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors
What happens to an eigenvector under its matrix transformation?
It is multiplied by a scalar.
It must rotate by a right angle.
It always becomes a unit vector.
It must become zero.
An eigenvector is a nonzero vector v with Av = λv. Its line is preserved; a negative λ reverses direction, and λ = 0 maps it to zero.
Av = λv
A must be square and v must be nonzero. The scalar λ is its eigenvalue.
Inner Product Spaces
What is special about the error in an orthogonal projection onto a subspace?
It is perpendicular to that subspace.
It is always a unit vector.
It lies in every direction of the subspace.
It is always zero.
The projected vector lies in the subspace, while the difference from the original vector is perpendicular to it.
projᵤ(v) = [(v · u)/(u · u)]u
This formula projects v onto the line spanned by a nonzero vector u in a Euclidean space.
Diagonalization and Quadratic Forms
When can an n by n matrix be diagonalized?
When it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.
Whenever it has n nonzero entries.
Whenever its determinant is zero.
Only when all eigenvalues are equal.
Independent eigenvectors form the columns of an invertible matrix P. In those coordinates, the transformation is represented by a diagonal matrix D.
A = PDP⁻¹
The columns of P are independent eigenvectors; the corresponding eigenvalues form D in the same order.
General Linear Transformations
Which rule must a linear transformation satisfy?
It preserves addition and scalar multiplication.
It sends every vector to itself.
It preserves every length.
It has to be invertible.
Linearity means combinations can be formed before or after applying the transformation, with the same result.
T(au + bv) = aT(u) + bT(v)
This must hold for all vectors u,v in the domain and all scalars a,b. The domain and codomain are vector spaces over the same field.
Numerical Methods
Why is a small residual alone not a guarantee of a small solution error?
An ill-conditioned matrix can amplify the error.
Residuals never depend on the computed solution.
A small residual means the system is inconsistent.
The solution error always equals the residual.
The residual measures how well the equations are satisfied. If A is nearly singular, a small mismatch can still correspond to a large change in the solution.
r = b − Ax
Here x is a computed approximation. The residual r measures the mismatch in the equations; conditioning determines how that mismatch relates to solution error.
differential-equations: In Euler’s method, which slope advances the current point?
The slope at the next, unknown point.
The average of all prior slopes.
The slope zero in every step.
Forward Euler uses the known current slope and step size h to estimate the next value.
yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + h f(xₙ,yₙ); xₙ₊₁ = xₙ + h
Approximation for y′ = f(x,y); smaller h often improves accuracy but stability still matters.
For y″ + ω²y = 0 with ω > 0, which family is the general solution?
Differentiating sine or cosine twice multiplies it by −ω², which makes y″ + ω²y equal zero.
ay″ + by′ + cy = 0 ⇒ ar² + br + c = 0
For constant coefficients and a ≠ 0; repeated and complex characteristic roots require their corresponding solution forms.
